title: Exploiting Student Parallelism for Low-latency GPU Inference of BERT-like Models in Online Services

problem.claim: Large BERT-like models have inefficient online GPU inference because model depth increases sequential computation and dynamic workloads incur batching and padding costs.

gap.claim: Efficient inference is needed for BERT-like models under real-world online workloads while preserving accuracy.

contributions.claim: Student Parallelism distills an original deep model into shallow, virtually stacked student models that run in parallel.
The approach uses adaptive student pruning to adjust the number of students for dynamic online workloads.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on real-world datasets and workloads report up to 4.1× lower latency while maintaining accuracy.
Experiments report up to 22.27× higher throughput during workload bursts.

narrative_sequence.summary: BERT-like models are widely used because of their high accuracy.
Large BERT-like models have inefficient online GPU inference due to sequential depth and dynamic workload overheads.
Student Parallelism uses stacked distillation, boosting ensembles, and parallel shallow students to reduce effective depth while maintaining accuracy.
Adaptive student pruning changes the student count for dynamic workloads, including reducing students during bursts.
The authors report lower latency and higher burst throughput in experiments.

source_observation.claim: Parallel shallow student models can provide low model depth while maintaining accuracy.

interpretation.claim: Distributing distilled computation across parallel components may reduce latency without requiring a single deep model.

application.claim: For latency-sensitive inference, consider distillation strategies that expose parallel execution.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this approach transfers to models, hardware, or workloads beyond those evaluated.

source_observation.claim: Adaptive pruning reduces the number of students during workload bursts with minimal reported accuracy loss.

interpretation.claim: Elastic computation can trade model parallelism for throughput under changing demand.

application.claim: Online inference systems may benefit from workload-aware adjustment of parallel capacity.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify the pruning policy, adaptation latency, or accuracy thresholds.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the evaluated datasets, hardware, baselines, or workload configurations.
The abstract does not quantify the accuracy retained or define the latency and throughput measurement conditions.
The abstract does not provide implementation details for stacking distillation, boosting ensemble, or adaptive pruning.
